flagged.evidence: id_roles.html, Trust policy: "A JSON policy document in which you define the principals that you trust to assume the role. A role trust policy is a required resource-based policy that is attached to a role in IAM."
flagged.problem: The fact is correct (answer true is right) and the explanation is accurate, but the statement nearly restates the term itself: a 'trust policy' identifies the principals 'trusted' to assume the role. A player can get it right from the name alone, so it teaches nothing about the design distinction that matters (trust policy = who can assume, permissions policy = what the role can do, and cross-account assumption also needs an identity-based allow in the caller's account).
flagged.suggestedFix: Rewrite to test the distinction, e.g. statement: "An IAM role's permissions policy determines which principals are allowed to assume the role." answer: false. Explanation: "The role's trust policy, a resource-based policy, specifies who can assume the role. The permissions policy specifies what the role session can do. For cross-account access, the caller also needs an identity-based policy that allows sts:AssumeRole on that role."

flagged.problem: Factually correct, but it only restates the textbook purpose of AWS WAF (SQL injection filtering) at difficulty 1; it does not test a design boundary. A Network Load Balancer is not a supported resource type; put an ALB or CloudFront in front of the application to use WAF." Source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/what-is-aws-waf.html
